paragraphs: A minimum spanning tree connects a collection of points with the smallest possible total edge weight. It is useful for hierarchical clustering, but even approximating it in an arbitrary metric space requires quadratic time in the number of points. This paper investigates how a useful initial collection of connections can change that computational picture.

The proposed framework first uses practical heuristics to build a forest: several separate trees. It then connects those trees using a low-weight set of additional edges. The authors prove that finding the optimal completion still requires quadratic time, but give a subquadratic algorithm with a 2.62 approximation factor for this completion problem.

The guarantee for the original spanning-tree problem depends on how much the initial forest overlaps with an optimal tree. Sufficiently useful heuristic information therefore supports faster approximation, with quality tied to that overlap. In experiments across many metrics, the framework produces nearly optimal trees while running orders of magnitude faster than exact algorithms.
icml-2025-approximate-forest-completion-.tldr: A two-stage spanning-tree framework uses heuristic forests to enable subquadratic approximation, with guarantees depending on overlap with an optimal tree.

paragraphs: Gradient descent needs a step size that balances progress against overshooting. A conventional choice uses a global smoothness constant, which describes how rapidly the objective's gradient can change. Armijo line-search instead chooses steps adaptively, responding to local behavior without requiring that global constant in advance.

Earlier theory established constant-factor improvements from this adaptation. This paper proves a stronger possibility: when an objective satisfies a particular non-uniform smoothness condition, line-search can improve the convergence rate itself. For the convex classification objectives covered by the analysis, including logistic regression and multiclass classification, it can achieve linear convergence where the fixed-step comparison converges sublinearly.

The authors also study nonconvex objectives satisfying gradient domination, including examples from policy optimization and generalized linear models. There, the method can match fast algorithms designed for those settings. A separate stochastic analysis covers convex losses under interpolation. Together, these results explain when a standard adaptive step-size rule can provide more than a modest speed improvement.
icml-2025-armijo-line-search-can-make-st.tldr: Under specified objective conditions, Armijo line-search improves gradient descent's convergence rate rather than merely its constant factors.

paragraphs: Designing an analog circuit topology means choosing a circuit structure that meets particular requirements. Automation is difficult because there are many possible structures and the constraints are strict. AUTOCIRCUIT-RL approaches this task with a language model trained to generate topologies from descriptions of the required design.

Training has two stages. Instruction tuning first teaches the model to respond to structured prompts that encode constraints. Reinforcement learning then refines its outputs using reward models that assess circuit validity, efficiency, and output voltage. After refinement, the model directly generates candidate topologies, bringing several design objectives into the training process.

The reported experiments show 12% more valid circuits, 14% better efficiency, and 38% fewer duplicate generations relative to the best baselines. With limited training data, valid-circuit synthesis succeeds more than 60% of the time. These findings support the framework's ability to generate useful, varied structures under the evaluated constraints, and provide empirical evidence for its potential to handle more complex circuit design.
icml-2025-autocircuit-rl-reinforcement-l.tldr: AUTOCIRCUIT-RL combines instruction tuning and reward-based refinement to improve the validity, efficiency, and diversity of generated analog circuits.

paragraphs: Evaluating a coding agent on real repository issues requires more than collecting problem descriptions. Its proposed patch must run in an environment consistent with the repository's historical dependencies, and tests must be executed and interpreted. That setup work has restricted benchmark coverage: the abstract identifies just 12 repositories in SWE-Bench.

The authors introduce SetUpAgent to automate historically accurate dependency setup, test execution, and result parsing. They use it to build SWEE-Bench, extending coverage to hundreds of repositories, and SWA-Bench, which emphasizes applications rather than libraries. Automation makes it practical to evaluate agents against a broader range of software projects.

The resulting datasets differ substantially from SWE-Bench. Their issues include less detailed descriptions and more complex fixes, and evaluated agents show success rates up to 60% lower. The findings indicate that benchmark composition can strongly affect apparent capability. Broader repository coverage therefore matters both for measuring progress and for deciding which coding-agent weaknesses deserve attention.
icml-2025-automated-benchmark-generation.tldr: SetUpAgent automates repository benchmark construction, revealing broader coding tasks on which evaluated agents have substantially lower success rates.

paragraphs: A language model can favor particular answers even when a question calls for an unbiased choice. This paper asks whether showing a model its previous answers to the same question helps it change those patterns. The study uses questions spanning nine topics and separates subjective, random, and objective requests.

The authors find that models can reduce bias during a multi-turn conversation when the question asks for a random, unbiased answer. That finding concerns a particular question type; it does not establish that response history removes every kind of bias. The paper also introduces B-score, a metric reported to detect biases across subjective, random, easy, and hard questions.

B-score additionally helps judge whether a model's answer should be accepted as correct or rejected as incorrect. On MMLU, HLE, and CSQA, it substantially improves verification accuracy over verbalized confidence and single-turn answer frequency alone. The results suggest that response history can supply useful evidence about reliability beyond what a model says about its own confidence.
icml-2025-b-score-detecting-biases-in-la.tldr: B-score uses response-history information to detect answer biases and improves answer verification over confidence statements and single-turn frequency.

paragraphs: Generating an entire backend application requires coordinating multiple functions and files while handling inputs from untrusted users. Success on isolated coding exercises does not directly establish this capability. BaxBench evaluates that broader challenge through 392 tasks asking language models to produce self-contained backend applications.

The benchmark examines functionality and security separately. Comprehensive tests check whether an application behaves as requested, while end-to-end exploits test whether it can actually be attacked. This distinction matters because an application can produce the expected outputs yet still expose a vulnerability when used in an adversarial way.

Among the evaluated models, OpenAI o1 has the highest correctness score at 62%. Averaged across the tested outputs for each model, exploits succeed against around half of the programs judged functionally correct. Models also struggle more with less popular backend frameworks. These findings show why application-level evaluation needs both functional tests and executable security checks: passing the former provides incomplete evidence that generated backend software is ready for use.
icml-2025-baxbench-can-llms-generate-cor.tldr: BaxBench finds substantial correctness and security failures when language models generate complete backend applications.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a vision transformer can require updating many parameters. Low-rank adaptation methods reduce that burden, but the authors argue that existing approaches overlook the higher-dimensional organization of multi-head attention weights. Canonical Rank Adaptation, or CaRA, makes that organization part of the adaptation method.

CaRA first represents transformer weights using two tensors: one for attention projection layers and another for feed-forward layers. It then applies low-rank updates in a Canonical-Polyadic Decomposition form. This is a tensor-based way to express adaptation compactly, allowing the method to reduce the number of parameters that must be trained.

The paper reports better performance than existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods on VTAB-1k and Fine-Grained Visual Categorization benchmarks. The contribution combines a different representation of transformer weights with an adaptation procedure suited to that representation. Its empirical findings suggest that preserving this higher-dimensional structure can make efficient tuning more effective on the evaluated visual classification tasks.
icml-2025-canonical-rank-adaptation-an-e.tldr: CaRA uses tensor-based low-rank updates to reduce trainable parameters and improve vision-transformer adaptation on the reported classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Optimal transport seeks a low-cost way to move one probability distribution into another. A Wasserstein barycenter extends this idea to finding a representative distribution for several inputs. This paper develops a method for computing both in high-dimensional spaces, where the optimization can be computationally demanding.

The method uses conditional normalizing flows to approximate input distributions through invertible transformations of a shared latent space. This representation makes it possible to minimize the transport cost directly with gradients. It provides an alternative to approaches built around dual formulations and complicated adversarial optimization.

For barycenters, the authors extend the approach through a conditional variance minimization problem. They identify the conditional architecture as central to handling hundreds of input distributions, a scale they describe as computationally infeasible for previous methods. Numerical experiments report accurate results on several high-dimensional tasks and favorable comparisons with earlier state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is therefore both an optimization formulation and a way to increase the number of distributions that can be combined.
icml-2025-computing-optimal-transport-ma.tldr: Conditional normalizing flows enable direct transport-cost optimization and barycenter computation for hundreds of high-dimensional input distributions.

paragraphs: The authors hypothesize that conventional regularization applied at individual samples contributes to neural networks' limited generalization. Deep Sturm–Liouville, or DSL, explores a different construction: applying continuous one-dimensional regularization along field lines that pass through the input space. The motivation is a hypothesis, while the proposed function approximator is a concrete implementation of that idea.

Along each field line, DSL solves a Sturm–Liouville problem to obtain orthogonal basis functions. It forms its predictions by combining those functions linearly. Neural networks parameterize both the vector field and the basis functions, and these components are learned together, allowing the regularized representation to adapt during training.

The paper connects this construction to a rank-one parabolic eigenvalue problem and trains it through stochastic gradient descent using implicit differentiation. Experiments show competitive performance on varied multivariate datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10. The results demonstrate the practicality of this mathematically structured approximator, including on high-dimensional images, without establishing that sample-based regularization explains all generalization failures.
icml-2025-deep-sturmliouville-from-sampl.tldr: DSL learns orthogonal basis functions along input-space field lines to introduce continuous one-dimensional regularization into a neural function approximator.

paragraphs: A neural functional network takes an entire neural network as its input. Such models need to respect symmetries involving permutations and scaling of that input's parameters. Existing parameter-sharing approaches offer lower memory use and faster execution than graph-based alternatives, but their equivariant linear layers have limited expressive power.

MAGEP-NFN keeps the parameter-sharing approach while introducing nonlinear equivariant layers expressed as polynomials of the input weights. This formulation incorporates additional relationships between weights in different hidden layers. The aim is to represent richer interactions while retaining the memory and runtime advantages that make parameter sharing attractive.

The authors report that the polynomial construction increases expressivity while keeping resource use low. Their experiments show competitive performance and efficiency against existing baselines. The central contribution is an architectural way to reconcile symmetry requirements with richer computations over network parameters. The empirical claim is competitiveness on the evaluated comparisons, rather than universal superiority over every alternative functional-network design.
icml-2025-equivariant-polynomial-functio.tldr: MAGEP-NFN uses equivariant polynomial layers to capture richer relationships between network weights while maintaining low memory use and runtime.

paragraphs: Protein design often specifies static structural properties, such as a motif or symmetry. This paper instead targets flexibility: how different parts of a protein can move. Because flexibility matters for activities including catalysis and molecular recognition, conditioning on it adds a dynamic property to the design objective.

The framework has two connected models. BackFlip predicts flexibility at each residue from a protein backbone. FliPS then uses BackFlip to tackle the inverse task, generating a backbone for a requested flexibility profile. FliPS is a conditional flow-matching model with SE(3) equivariance, preserving the appropriate behavior under rotations and translations.

In the reported experiments, FliPS generates novel and diverse backbones with the desired flexibility, which the authors verify using molecular dynamics simulations. This supports the feasibility of directing structure generation through a movement-related target. The demonstrated result concerns backbone flexibility; the motivation from protein function explains why that control is useful without equating a matching flexibility profile with demonstrated catalytic or recognition performance.
icml-2025-flexibility-conditioned-protei.tldr: BackFlip and FliPS connect flexibility prediction with protein-backbone generation, producing target flexibility profiles verified through molecular dynamics simulations.

paragraphs: Applications usually work with character strings, while modern language models assign probabilities to sequences of tokens. That mismatch can make seemingly minor prompt details consequential. For example, whether a prompt ends with a space can change its tokenization and therefore how the token-level model processes it.

This paper develops algorithms that convert a token-level language model into a character-level one. It provides both exact procedures and approximations, giving different ways to handle the computation needed for this conversion. The objective is to expose a distribution over the text representation applications actually use while starting from an existing token-based model.

Experiments on four publicly available language models assess runtime and approximation accuracy. The authors find that even a small computational budget can yield an accurate character-level approximation at reasonably fast speeds. They also report a significant improvement in compression measured in bits per byte. These results indicate that changing how a model's distribution is represented can have practical benefits for text probabilities and compression.
icml-2025-from-language-models-over-toke.tldr: Exact and approximate conversion algorithms expose character-level distributions from token-based language models, with reported gains in compression.

paragraphs: Graph edit distance measures how much editing is needed to transform one graph into another. Computing its optimum is NP-hard, so practical methods often approximate it. Neural approximators can be effective, but the paper highlights costly ground-truth requirements, limited interpretability, and expensive retraining when moving between graph domains.

GRAIL uses a language model and automated prompt tuning to generate a program that computes an approximation. This changes what is learned: the output is an executable procedure rather than a neural predictor of the distance. The authors describe the approach as interpretable end to end and capable of autonomous improvement without ground-truth supervision.

Experiments across seven datasets show better prediction quality than the compared state-of-the-art approximation methods, alongside strong transfer across different graph distributions. These findings support program generation as a practical route to graph comparison. The method still addresses an approximation problem; its reported improvements concern the quality and transferability of the generated procedures rather than making optimal graph edit distance inexpensive.
icml-2025-grail-graph-edit-distance-and-.tldr: GRAIL generates interpretable graph-edit-distance programs with language models and prompt tuning, improving approximation quality and cross-domain transfer in experiments.

paragraphs: Imitation learning aims to learn behavior from expert demonstrations. SOAR provides an algorithmic template that alternates between updating a cost function and updating a policy in a primal-dual procedure. Its main change concerns how the policy update handles uncertainty while deciding what behavior to explore.

Within that update, SOAR uses an actor-critic method with multiple critics. Their estimates provide information about critic uncertainty, which is used to construct an optimistic critic that drives exploration. This connects exploration to uncertainty in the learned evaluations instead of treating the policy update as a fixed component of the imitation-learning procedure.

For a tabular setting, the framework yields an algorithm called FRA whose guarantees match the best known dependence on the accuracy parameter epsilon. In practical evaluations, SOAR consistently improves the tested primal-dual imitation-learning algorithms built on actor-critic updates. The authors report approximately halving the episodes needed to reach the same performance. The theory and experiments thus support the template at different levels: formal accuracy dependence and observed interaction efficiency.
icml-2025-il-soar-imitation-learning-wit.tldr: SOAR uses uncertainty from multiple critics to guide imitation-learning exploration, approximately halving required episodes in the reported practical evaluations.

paragraphs: Raising a language model's decoding temperature is a common way to seek more varied outputs. This paper examines why that adjustment may fail to increase meaningful coverage, even though lowering temperature can improve output quality. It frames the distinction through precision, representing quality, and recall, representing coverage.

Using a simple but common case, the authors analyze what temperature adjustment can accomplish. Their analysis indicates that effective temperature tuning requires training that already encourages coverage. Changing the sampling setting alone therefore may not provide the desired range of good outputs when the training objective has not supported that range.

The proposed response is to rethink training losses through the precision-recall framework. The reported results show a substantially better quality-coverage trade-off than negative log-likelihood training combined with temperature scaling. The contribution connects a generation-time control to the objective used during learning: improving diversity may require changing what the model learns, as well as how its outputs are sampled.
icml-2025-improving-diversity-in-languag.tldr: Training losses that encourage coverage improve the precision-recall trade-off beyond what temperature scaling alone achieves in the reported results.

paragraphs: A deterministic tokenizer assigns a particular token sequence to a character string. Yet a token-level language model can assign probability to other sequences that decode to the same text. These noncanonical sequences never arise from that tokenizer in training, but the paper identifies exponentially many such encodings for each character string.

The authors propose restricting positive probability to canonical sequences. One approach enforces the restriction through conditioning at inference time, without additional training. The other builds it into the model's parameterization, guaranteeing canonical outputs but requiring training. These provide two different ways to align the model's output space with the tokenizer's actual behavior.

Across several models and corpora, correcting canonicality mistakes improves held-out data likelihood. The result shows that tokenization consistency has a measurable consequence for probability allocation. By eliminating token sequences that the deterministic encoding process would never produce, the methods redirect probability toward the canonical representation used by the data, with empirical benefits for the evaluated language models.
icml-2025-language-models-over-canonical.tldr: Enforcing canonical token encodings prevents probability allocation to tokenizer-impossible sequences and improves held-out likelihood in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A well-behaved generative model can be represented as a deterministic transformation of Gaussian noise into data. Drawing ordinary samples is then straightforward, but drawing samples that also satisfy an additional constraint is generally intractable. This paper moves that conditional sampling problem into the model's underlying noise space.

The authors train diffusion samplers over noise variables using reinforcement learning. Training aims to make the samples, after passing through the original generator, follow the desired posterior distribution in data space. Learning a sampler amortizes the inference cost, and the paper observes that the noise-space posterior is smoother for many models and constraints.

The method supports conditional sampling from unconditional GAN, VAE, hierarchical VAE, and flow-based priors. Experiments with large pretrained models cover conditional image generation, reinforcement learning with human feedback, and protein structure generation, with favorable comparisons to other inference methods. The central idea is to use a generator's noise representation as the place to learn constrained sampling, taking advantage of smoother posterior structure when it is present.
icml-2025-outsourced-diffusion-sampling-.tldr: Outsourced diffusion sampling learns posterior samplers in a generator's noise space, enabling conditional generation from existing unconditional models.

paragraphs: A robot benefits from predicting how objects and scenes will change, but many video-prediction methods require precise action labels. PlaySlot learns from unlabeled video sequences instead. It extracts representations of individual objects together with latent actions that describe the changes observed between frames.

Those representations support predictions of future object states and video frames. The model can generate different possible futures depending on the latent actions supplied. Actions may be inferred from video dynamics, provided by a user, or produced by a learned policy, making the same predictive model useful under several forms of control.

The authors report better video prediction than the evaluated stochastic and object-centric baselines across different environments. They also show that the inferred actions support sample-efficient learning of robot behaviors from unlabeled video demonstrations. The contribution links observation and control: a video supplies more than examples of appearance, because its dynamics can also provide an action representation for predicting and learning behavior.
icml-2025-playslot-learning-inverse-late.tldr: PlaySlot learns objects and latent actions from unlabeled videos to support controllable future prediction and sample-efficient robot behavior learning.

paragraphs: Message-passing graph networks emphasize local interactions, which can make it difficult to capture structural properties such as connectivity and cycles. Positional encodings add information about location within a graph. Persistent homology adds topological information across multiple resolutions. This paper investigates how these two sources of structural information compare.

The theoretical result is that neither approach dominates the other in expressivity. The authors construct cases where positional encoding succeeds and persistent homology fails, and other cases with the reverse outcome. This establishes complementary strengths, rather than showing that the two methods encode equivalent information.

These insights motivate PiPE, a learnable persistence-informed positional encoding method. The authors prove that it is more expressive than either approach in their analysis. They also report strong performance on molecule property prediction, graph classification, and out-of-distribution generalization. The work connects a formal comparison of structural representations to a model design that uses their complementary information, with empirical evidence across several graph-learning tasks.
icml-2025-positional-encoding-meets-pers.tldr: PiPE combines complementary positional and topological graph information, with stronger theoretical expressivity and strong reported task performance.

paragraphs: When a language model chooses an answer or a tool, uncertainty can be represented by a set of plausible choices. Conformal prediction constructs such a set with high-probability coverage of the true answer. This paper uses that set to revise the decision problem presented to the model.

Conformal revision of questions, or CROQ, removes choices outside the prediction set and asks the model the narrowed question. The motivation is that fewer alternatives may improve accuracy. Since large prediction sets leave little to prune, the authors also introduce CP-OPT, which learns scores designed to reduce set size while maintaining coverage.

Experiments on MMLU, ToolAlpaca, and TruthfulQA with multiple language models show that CROQ improves accuracy over standard inference, with larger gains when combined with CP-OPT. The results connect uncertainty estimation to a practical inference procedure. Coverage concerns the retained answer set, while the observed accuracy gains concern the model's subsequent choice from that set; they are related but distinct outcomes.
icml-2025-prune-n-predict-optimizing-llm.tldr: CROQ improves tested LLM decisions by re-asking questions with conformal prediction sets, especially when CP-OPT learns smaller sets while maintaining coverage.

paragraphs: Biomedical modeling draws on heterogeneous data sources and a wide variety of therapeutic tasks. PyTDC addresses the infrastructure needed to train, evaluate, and run models across that landscape. The open-source platform brings together distributed, continuously updated data and model weights while standardizing benchmarking and inference interfaces.

The paper describes this architecture and presents a case study on a newly introduced single-cell drug-target nomination task. The evaluation finds that both state-of-the-art graph representation methods and domain-specific graph-theoretic methods perform poorly. This makes the task a concrete test of whether existing modeling approaches can handle the relevant biological context.

A context-aware geometric deep learning model outperforms the evaluated alternatives, but it cannot generalize to unseen cell types or incorporate additional modalities. Those are specific shortcomings revealed by the study. PyTDC's contribution is therefore both operational and investigative: it provides a shared modeling workflow and demonstrates how that workflow can expose research needs in multimodal, context-aware biomedical AI.
icml-2025-pytdc-a-multimodal-machine-lea.tldr: PyTDC unifies biomedical model workflows and uses a single-cell drug-target task to reveal gaps in context generalization and multimodal modeling.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning often assigns model-generated labels to unlabeled examples and uses them for further training. A confidence threshold decides which pseudolabels to accept. However, a high confidence score can be misleading when the model is overconfident or poorly calibrated, allowing inaccurate labels into the training process.

This paper learns both confidence scores and thresholds through a framework with an explicit error-control parameter. It addresses the reliability of the scores as well as the acceptance rule. That gives practitioners a principled way to manage the balance between accepting more pseudolabels and maintaining their quality.

Integrated with modern semi-supervised learning methods, the framework produces significant improvements in accuracy and training efficiency in the reported experiments. The authors also examine how choices of the error parameter relate to final model performance. The contribution turns pseudolabel selection into a controlled quality-quantity trade-off, helping explain why choosing a threshold in isolation may leave a central source of training error unresolved.
icml-2025-rethinking-confidence-scores-a.tldr: Jointly learning confidence scores and thresholds with an error-control parameter improves pseudolabel selection, accuracy, and training efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Softmax allows neural networks to make differentiable selections among alternatives, making it central to query-key lookups. A sharply focused selection can look like a reliable computational rule. This paper asks whether that sharp behavior persists when the number of input items grows beyond the sizes encountered during training.

The authors prove a limitation: even for a task as simple as selecting the maximum key, learned softmax circuitry disperses as problem size increases. They attribute this to softmax's inability to robustly approximate sharp functions as the number of alternatives grows. Thus, sharp behavior at one input size does not by itself establish robust size generalization.

The paper proposes adapting temperature during inference as an ad hoc way to improve sharpness. This is presented as a technique for improvement, rather than a general resolution of the theoretical limitation. The contribution clarifies why a seemingly crisp learned selection mechanism can become less decisive on larger inputs, and identifies temperature adaptation as one practical response to that problem.
icml-2025-softmax-is-not-enough-for-shar.tldr: Softmax-based selections lose sharpness as input size grows, and adaptive inference-time temperature is proposed as a partial practical remedy.

paragraphs: The sliced-Wasserstein distance compares probability distributions while capturing geometric information at a manageable computational cost. It is used in applications such as generative modeling and domain adaptation. This paper studies what happens when that distance serves as an optimization objective, focusing on the critical points that training may encounter.

The authors analyze stability by explicitly constructing perturbations. Their main stated result is that stable critical points cannot concentrate on segments. This excludes a particular geometric form for stable solutions, providing information about the optimization landscape beyond simply knowing that the distance is computationally convenient.

The paper also investigates the existence of critical points and their convergence behavior, and uses numerical experiments to illustrate the theory. These results matter because the geometry and stability of critical points help explain how optimization can behave for models trained with this objective. The contribution is a structural analysis of possible optimization outcomes, rather than a blanket guarantee that every training procedure reaches its desired distribution.
icml-2025-towards-understanding-gradient.tldr: A critical-point analysis shows that stable sliced-Wasserstein solutions cannot concentrate on segments, clarifying part of the objective's optimization geometry.

paragraphs: A neural network's computational graph determines how information can travel through its computations. Poor connectivity can leave information unable to reach where it is needed or force too much through restricted routes. These effects can prevent learning certain functions, making graph structure an important architectural choice.

This paper focuses on feedforward computational graphs: directed graphs without backward edges. Much prior analysis concerns undirected graphs, so its conclusions do not directly settle which feedforward structures are desirable. The authors identify two complementary measures, fidelity and mixing time, and use them to examine several popular graph choices.

The study combines theoretical analysis of how these measures behave as graphs scale with empirical comparisons to trained-network performance. The observed correlations connect structural properties to downstream results. The contribution provides a way to reason about feedforward graph design through multiple measures, supported by both mathematical and experimental evidence, rather than treating one graph statistic as a complete explanation of model quality.
icml-2025-what-makes-a-good-feedforward-.tldr: Fidelity and mixing time provide complementary measures for analyzing feedforward computational graphs and their relationship to trained-network performance.
